title: ICE Arrests Rise Across California as Election Nears, Community Groups Report
excerpt: A reported 45-day enforcement surge, dubbed Operation Safe California, coincides with detention data showing arrests up sharply year on year — and with warnings from advocates that visible enforcement could chill immigrant communities days before the November 3 midterms.
body:
• Reports of increased ICE arrests across California have multiplied in the final weeks before the November 3 midterm elections, from Los Angeles to the Central Valley and San Diego area.
  • ICE nationwide arrests nearly doubled in July 2026 to 41,850, from 24,222 in July 2025, according to Deportation Data Project figures; arrests in the San Francisco region rose from 1,556 to 2,495 across May-July year on year.
  • Community groups attribute the latest spike to a reported 45-day surge, "Operation Safe California," which DHS has not publicly announced; a DHS spokesperson declined to disclose arrest numbers.
  • If you are in an affected community: advocates urge families to have a care plan for children and documents in order; enforcement concerns do not establish that operations were designed to influence voting.

Dozens of immigrants have been arrested by federal immigration agents across Southern California this week, including in Los Angeles County, as news of a potential mass enforcement operation in California sent immigrant defense groups scrambling to monitor agents' activity, according to LA Public Press. From Pacoima to Bellflower, and from East LA to the Fashion District, Department of Homeland Security agents have arrested dozens of immigrants since Monday, according to LA Taco reporting cited by the outlet.

A Surge in the Data, Not Just the Headlines

The recent reports sit on top of a measurable escalation. Nationwide, ICE nearly doubled arrests in July 2026 compared to July 2025 — 41,850 from 24,222 — according to the Deportation Data Project, a collaboration between researchers at UCLA and UC Berkeley, reported by Voices of Monterey Bay. Arrests for the three months spanning May to July in the San Francisco region, which includes Monterey County, jumped from 1,556 in 2025 to 2,495 in 2026.

https://www.instagram.com/reel/DeuNDobCHKZ/

Advocates describe a "shadow surge" that ran quietly through the summer — including cases in which detained people's families could not find any record of the detention through rapid-response networks — followed by a more public surge coinciding with the end of the harvest season's peak and the approaching midterms. Reported tactics include surveillance and targeted arrests of people whose humanitarian protection has ended, and moving detainees in ways that complicate access to legal aid.

Operation Safe California

The spike in arrests comes as news broke about "Operation Safe California," a reported 45-day surge by DHS targeting immigrants with and without criminal records, according to sources who spoke with the Washington Examiner. The operation has not been publicly announced by DHS. At least 45 people, and as many as 80, have been arrested across Southern California since Monday, when the surge reportedly began, according to LA Taco.

Asked for the number of arrests in the LA region during the surge, a DHS spokesperson told LA Public Press the agency would not disclose details: "For operational security and the safety of our officers, ICE will not disclose or discuss law enforcement operations. Every day, DHS enforces the laws of the nation across the country including in California."

Election Timing and State Pushback

The timing, weeks before the November 3, 2026 midterm elections, has drawn scrutiny. Some Democratic lawmakers and immigrant rights organizations have raised concerns that visible enforcement activity could discourage participation among eligible voters in affected communities — though those concerns do not establish that the operations were designed to influence the election. California lawmakers are requesting information about arrests, operational procedures and due process protections, and recently signed state legislation expands detention oversight and transparency while leaving federal immigration authority intact. Immigrant defense groups are urging people vulnerable to arrest to stay home if possible and to make a plan for the care of loved ones in the event they are detained.
